why: offset everywhere incl. toc and CLI, validated, documented and tested
prompt:
Add a `heading_offset` option to `markdown.Markdown` (and `markdown.markdown`): a whole number from 0 to 5, default 0, that shifts the level of every heading Markdown produces by that many (an `h1` becomes an `h2` with 1), never beyond `h6`. Any other value raises `ValueError`.
- It applies to hash and underline headings, and to headings from extensions such as `md_in_html`.
- The `toc` extension sees the shifted levels (its tokens and `toc_depth`).
- The command line gets `--heading-offset N`.

Work on your own; nobody will answer questions. When you finish, report: status `done` if you did the task, `not_found` if something the task names does not exist, `blocked` if you could not do it; `answer` holds any answer the task asks for (otherwise one short sentence); `changed` lists the files you changed.

report.answer: I added `heading_offset` (a whole number from 0 to 5, default 0) to `markdown.Markdown` and `markdown.markdown`, and `--heading-offset N` to the command line. All 1143 tests pass, with 112 skipped. A new built-in tree processor shifts every heading after parsing and before `toc`, never past `h6`, so `toc` tokens and `toc_depth` see the shifted levels. This covers hash and underline headings, headings in footnotes, and `md_in_html` headings: Markdown inside an HTML block, and HTML headings marked with the `markdown` attribute. Raw HTML headings that pass through unparsed stay as written. Values like 1.0, True and '1' also raise `ValueError`. The command line rejects other values with a usage error instead of a traceback. The command-line options now always include `heading_offset` (0 if not given), and I updated the existing option tests to match.
